title: A household emergency plan that gets practiced
h1: A household emergency plan that actually gets practiced
dek: Five decisions, one page, and a rehearsal schedule small enough to survive a busy year. What FEMA, the CDC and the Red Cross say a plan needs, where they differ, and how to think about the first hour, the first 72 hours and the first two weeks.
description: Build a household emergency plan from Ready.gov, FEMA and CDC guidance: five decisions, a contact plan, a needs checklist, practice ideas and the first 72 hours.
recheck: If Ready.gov or the CDC revise their planning pages, or at the next quarterly source sweep.

source_use.start-ready-plan: The four steps (meet, assess household needs, document, practice), the five starting questions and the list of household factors to consider.
source_use.ready-are-you-ready: Assess the situation, then decide to stay or change location; communication plan with an out-of-state contact reachable two ways; wallet or digital copy for everyone; meeting places in several directions; practice like a fire drill; six-month refresh; one-year timeline; documents and cash guidance; school plans.
source_use.start-cdc-pyh-connected: At least two meeting places; texts often go through when calls do not; plan for children, older adults and pets; microchip pets.
source_use.start-cdc-disability-plan: Contact list of the people who support your health, with arrangements for them to check on you; use pictures; practice, review every year and share the plan.
source_use.start-redcross-older-adults: Build and meet with a support network; plan to stay home at least two weeks or evacuate; review, practice and refresh every six months.
source_use.start-ready-alerts: How Wireless Emergency Alerts, the Emergency Alert System, NOAA Weather Radio and the FEMA App differ, and the limits of each.
source_use.start-ready-financial: Small bills of cash, insurance, document storage and benefits by direct deposit.
source_use.start-ready-evacuation: Several possible destinations, and finding a pet-friendly place in advance because most public shelters allow only service animals.
source_use.start-ready-kit: The NOAA Weather Radio item on the kit list, and the current page's 're-think your needs every year' interval.
source_use.cdc-water-store: Water baseline of 1 gallon per person per day for 3 days with 2 weeks as the goal.
source_use.start-ready-disability: A weather radio with a text display and flashing alert for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.
source_use.start-ready-low-cost: The free and low-cost starting points (free communication plan, free resources, local alerts, evacuation plan).
